abstract: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as a new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 4–8-step regime down to just 1–2 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely a stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation. Project page: chendaryen.github.io/NitroFusion2.

sections.body: The paper revisits which features adversarial distillation discriminators read. In an MMDiT, text-token states interact with image tokens through joint attention, so they depend on the sample. **TSAD** attaches discriminator heads to these intermediate text-token states. **ACD** conditions the discriminator on one of six structured aspect fields (typography, object, style, background, action, or layout) or on the full caption, sampled at each training step. The stated claims are that text-stream discrimination outperforms image-stream discrimination across all evaluated benchmarks, that aspect cues yield aspect-specific gains, and that two-step results are competitive with alternatives.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Adversarial distillation has read only image features, and MMDiT text tokens offer an unused alternative.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into three lines. Few-step methods include progressive distillation, consistency models, distribution matching distillation, and MeanFlow, and the authors state that one- and two-step generation remains challenging. Adversarial diffusion distillation attaches discriminator heads to a frozen encoder or to teacher tokens, and NitroFusion uses an ensemble of expert heads. Text-conditioned GANs, including GigaGAN, condition the discriminator on text while its features still come from the image. Analyses of joint attention show that text-stream positions absorb image content, but these states have been used for analysis and inference-time control, not as the feature space for adversarial supervision.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work conditions discriminators on text but reads adversarial features only from the image.

sections.body: The student is trained against a frozen MMDiT discriminator backbone with a hinge loss, using lightweight heads on intermediate states. **TSAD** reads text-stream attention outputs. Because the image-attention contribution enters these outputs, they depend on the image, unlike fixed cross-attention text embeddings. Heads sit at selected layers, and image-stream heads are trained alongside them, with loss weights of 0.1 for the image-stream term and 0.1 for the flow-matching term. **ACD** builds six image-grounded aspect fields per reference, samples one valid cue uniformly at each step, conditions the backbone on it, and routes text-stream scores to cue-specific heads. The cue requires no additional backbone evaluation. The training data is a synthetic set of 100k reference images generated with Z-Image-Turbo.
sections.heading: Approach
sections.headline: TSAD attaches heads to text-stream attention outputs, and ACD picks one aspect cue per training step.

sections.body: Both the student and the discriminator backbone are initialized from Z-Image-Turbo, and the backbone stays frozen. Benchmarks are LongText-Bench in English and Chinese, OneIG-Bench, GenEval, and DPG-Bench. At one step, NitroFusion2 leads all evaluated baselines, improving LongText-EN and LongText-CN over TwinFlow by 14.2 and 10.9 points. Against the eight-step Z-Image-Turbo reference it scores 86.48 against 84.86 on DPG-Bench and 75.86 against 75.01 on GenEval, while a substantial gap remains on text rendering. At two steps it leads four of six GenEval categories, but Z-Image-Turbo++ scores higher on some metrics. In 1,000-step ablations, LongText-EN is 22.31 for text-stream, 17.86 for image-stream, and 24.47 for both.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: At one step, NitroFusion2 leads all five benchmarks and is on par with an eight-step reference on GenEval.

sections.body: The conclusion states that MMDiT text-token states work as an effective adversarial representation. TSAD gives particularly strong gains in text rendering, and ACD gives targeted control and better overall balance than full-prompt conditioning. The authors describe the text stream as steerable rather than fixed. The stated limitations are that complex scenes remain challenging, especially at one step; sample diversity is reduced; ACD shows a seesaw effect, where emphasizing one aspect can weaken others; and layer selection is supported empirically rather than established as optimal. Listed future directions include balancing the seesaw effect and studying how text-stream information evolves across depth.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Limitations
sections.headline: Remaining limits are complex scenes at one step, reduced sample diversity, and a seesaw effect across cues.

sections.body: The authors state that they used generative AI tools and LLMs to generate synthetic datasets, implement methods, give feedback on methodology and experiments, interpret results, draft and edit parts of the paper, and create and modify figures. They state that these tools were not used to propose or refine hypotheses or to develop the conceptual framework. The statement says every reported number comes from a run the authors launched and verified, and that the authors are responsible for all content, including AI-assisted content.
sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.headline: The AI use statement says generative tools supported data, implementation, drafting and figures, not hypotheses or framework.

sections.body: The statement points to where the method is defined: Sections 3.2 and 3.3, and the training objective in Section 3.5. Appendix A gives the training setup, Section A.1 lists the seven cue categories, and Section A.2 lists the layers each set of heads reads. Dataset construction, including the annotation model and the six structured-caption fields, is described in Section 3.4. Appendix C is cited for one full training step as pseudo-code. The statement says NitroFusion2 will be released publicly upon acceptance.
sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.headline: The reproducibility statement points to method sections, training setup, cue list, pseudo-code, and public release upon acceptance.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the training setup: Adam with beta1 0.0 and beta2 0.9, a batch size of 256 on eight H100 GPUs, and 20,000 steps in two stages, the first 5,000 off-policy and the remaining 15,000 on-policy. Discriminator heads follow APT, with a pool of three heads per stream and per cue, one drawn at random per step, and periodic re-initialization. Table 5 lists the seven cue categories. Table 7 shows the selected text-stream taps lead on four of five metrics, with GenEval the exception. Appendix B gives OneIG and DPG-Bench breakdowns. Table 10 compares open-weight models sampled under identical settings; at one step NitroFusion2 leads four of five benchmarks, trailing on LongText-CN.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the training setup, cue categories, layer choices, per-dimension results, and open-weight comparisons.
